[[File:Disk graph in the plane.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|A graph with sphericity {{math|2}}: A space graph of the vertices of a pentagon, realized as the intersection graph of the unit {{math|2}}-disks in the plane, centered on these points. This is also known as a unit disk graph.]]

In the mathematical field of [[graph theory]], the '''sphericity''' of a [[Graph theory|graph]] is a [[Graph property|graph invariant]] defined to be the smallest [[dimension]] of [[Euclidean space]] required to realize the graph as the [[intersection graph]] of [[Congruence (geometry)|congruent]] [[sphere]]s.<ref>{{harvtxt|Fishburn|1983|page=309|loc=Section 1}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Maehara|1986|page=311}}</ref> The sphericity of a graph is one of several notions of graph dimension based on intersection graphs; others include [[boxicity]] and [[cubicity]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Roberts|1969|pages=301–310}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Maehara|1986|page=311}}: "As a similar type of graph-dimension, there are the boxicity and the cubicity.".</ref> The concept of sphericity was first introduced by Hiroshi Maehara in 1980<ref>{{harvtxt|Maehara|1984|page=55|loc="Received 1980"}}</ref> (and also used by Timothy F. Havel in 1982).<ref>{{harvtxt|Fishburn|1983|pages=309–310|loc=Section 1}}</ref>

== Definitions ==
This article only considers [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|undirected graphs]], with finite and non-empty vertex sets, with no loop and no multiple edge.<ref>{{harvtxt|Maehara|1984|page=55|loc=Section 1}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Fishburn|1983|page=309|loc=Section 1}}</ref>

The ''sphericity'' of a graph <math>G</math>, denoted by <math>\operatorname{sph}(G)</math>, is the smallest [[integer]] <math>k \geq 0</math> such that <math>G</math> can be realized as the intersection graph of [[Closed set|closed]] unit-diameter spheres,<ref>{{harvtxt|Fishburn|1983|page=309|loc=Section 1}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Maehara|1986|page=311}}</ref> in the <math>k</math>-dimensional Euclidean space, <math>\mathbb{R}^k</math>.

Sphericity can also be defined using the language of space graphs as follows. For a [[finite set]] of points in the <math>k</math>-dimensional Euclidean space, a ''space graph'' <math>\mathbb G</math> is built by connecting pairs of points with a [[line segment]] if and only if their [[Euclidean distance]] is less than some specified constant (called the ''adjacency limit'' of <math>\mathbb G</math>).<ref>{{harvtxt|Maehara|1984|page=55|loc=Section 1}}</ref><br>Then, the sphericity of a graph <math>G</math> is the minimum integer <math>k \geq 0</math> such that <math>G</math> is [[Isomorphism|isomorphic]] to a space graph in <math>\mathbb{R}^k</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Maehara|1984|page=55|loc=Section 1}}</ref> Indeed: A space graph in <math>k</math>-space is, as an abstract graph, nothing but the intersection graph of a family of equiradial <math>k</math>-disks in <math>k</math>-space.<ref>{{harvtxt|Maehara|1984|page=55|loc=Section 1}}</ref> Remark: Maehara takes these disks to be [[Open set|open]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Maehara|1984|page=55|loc=Section 1}}: "[…] we connect each pair <math>x_i, x_j, i \neq j</math>, by a line segment whenever <math>\| x_i - x_j \| < t</math>, […]".<br>(I.e., <math>\| m_{ij} - x_i \| < t/2</math> and <math>\| m_{ij} - x_j \| < t/2</math>, where <math>m_{ij} = (x_i + x_j)/2</math>.)</ref> (The final result is the same.)

[[File:Indifference graph = unit interval graph.svg|thumb|310px|A space graph with sphericity {{math|1}}, formed from a set of points on the real [[number line]], by connecting pairs of points whose distance is at most {{math|1}}. Also the intersection graph of the set of unit {{math|1}}-disks, i.e. unit intervals, centered on the points.]]

Graphs of sphericity <math>1</math> are known as [[unit interval graph]]s<ref>{{harvtxt|Maehara|1984|page=55|loc=Section 1}}: "The graphs of sphericity <math>1</math> are intersection graphs of families of unit intervals, […].".</ref> or [[indifference graph]]s. Graphs of sphericity <math>2</math> are known as [[unit disk graph]]s.

== Values on certain graph classes, bounds ==
The sphericity on certain graph classes can be computed exactly. The following sphericities were given by Maehara in his original paper on the topic<ref>{{harvtxt|Maehara|1984|pages=55–56|loc=Section 1}}</ref> (<math>n</math> denotes the [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph order]]).

|+
!Graph
!Description
!Sphericity
!Note
|-
|<math>K_1</math>
|[[Complete graph]]
|<math>0</math>
|
|-
|<math>K_n</math>
|Complete graph
|<math>1</math>
|<math>n > 1</math>
|-
|<math>P_n</math>
|[[Path graph]]
|<math>1</math>
|<math>n > 1</math>
|-
|<math>C_n</math>
|[[Cycle graph|Circuit graph]]
|<math>2</math>
|<math>n > 3</math>
|-
|<math>K_{p(2)}</math>
|[[Multipartite graph|Complete multipartite graph]] on <math>p</math> parts of [[Cardinal number|cardinal]] <math>2</math>
|<math>2</math>
|<math>p > 1.</math><ref>{{harvtxt|Fishburn|1983|page=310|loc=Section 1}}</ref>
|}

However, Fishburn claims that <math>\operatorname{cub}(G) = \operatorname{sph}(G) = 0</math> if and only if <math>G</math> is a complete graph (where <math>\operatorname{cub}(G)</math> denotes the [[cubicity]] of <math>G</math>; by convention, <math>0</math>-space is the [[Singleton (mathematics)|singleton]] <math>\{ 0 \}</math> and any (closed) <math>0</math>-disk = any (closed) <math>0</math>-cube = <math>\{ 0 \}</math>), and that <math>\operatorname{cub}(G) = \operatorname{sph}(G) = 1</math> if and only if <math>G</math> is a unit interval graph that is not complete.<ref>{{harvtxt|Fishburn|1983|page=310|loc=Section 1}}</ref> Indeed, his definition of cubicity / sphericity allows adjacent distinct vertices with same closed neighborhood to be assigned the same cube / sphere.<ref>{{harvtxt|Fishburn|1983|page=314|loc=Section 3}}: "Figure 2 shows […]; the lined circles in the four corners are for [the <math>B</math> vertices] <math>b_1, b_3, b_7,</math> and <math>b_9,</math> which are respectively equivalent to the four corner <math>A</math> vertices.".</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Roberts|1969|page=303|loc=Section 2}}: "[…], two points [<math>a</math> and <math>b</math>] are equivalent if and only if they have the same «closed neighborhoods». […] (Map <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> onto the same point in <math>n</math>-space.)".</ref>

Maehara conjectured that the graphs of the <math>7</math>-prism, <math>8</math>-prism, and <math>9</math>-prism have sphericity <math>3</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Maehara|1986|page=312}}</ref>

The most general upper bound on sphericity that is known is as follows:<br>If a graph <math>G</math> is not [[Complete graph|complete]], then <math>\operatorname{sph}(G) \leq |G| - \mathbb{\text{ω}}(G)</math>,<br>where <math>|G|</math> and <math>\mathbb{\text{ω}}(G)</math> respectively denote the order and the [[Clique (graph theory)|clique number]] of <math>G</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Maehara|1984|page=57|loc=Section 2, Theorem 2}}</ref><ref>For a complete graph <math>G</math> of any order <math>n \geq 1</math>, <math>~ |G| - \mathbb{\text{ω}}(G) = 0</math>. With Fishburn's definition of sphericity, for a complete graph <math>G</math> of any order <math>n \geq 1</math>, <math>~ \operatorname{sph}(G) = 0</math>. Then, <math>\operatorname{sph}(G) \leq |G| - \mathbb{\text{ω}}(G)</math> extends to complete graphs (not only to <math>K_1</math>).</ref>

For certain graphs, a slightly smaller upper bound is known:<br>If <math>G</math> is a [[split graph]] and <math>|G| - \mathbb{\mbox{ω}}(G) > 2</math>, then <math>\operatorname{sph}(G) \leq |G| - \mathbb{\mbox{ω}}(G) - 1</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Maehara|1984|page=58|loc=Section 3, Theorem 3}}</ref>

For every [[Natural number|positive integer]] <math>m</math>, there exists a split graph <math>G</math> such that <math>\operatorname{sph}(G) = |G| - \mathbb{\text{ω}}(G) - 1 = m</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Maehara|1984|page=59|loc=Section 3, Theorem 4}}</ref>

For <math>1 \leq m \leq n</math>, <math>~ \operatorname{sph}(K_{m,n}) \leq m - 1 + \lceil n/2 \rceil</math>, where <math>K_{m,n}</math> denotes the [[complete bipartite graph]] with part cardinals <math>m</math> and <math>n</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Maehara|1984|page=63|loc=Section 5, Theorem 6}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Fishburn|1983|page=310|loc=Section 1}} mentions a different version:<br>" <math>\operatorname{sph}(K_{m,n}) \leq m + \lfloor n/2 \rfloor</math> ".<br>For odd <math>n</math>, <math>~~ m - 1 + \lceil n/2 \rceil = m + \lfloor n/2 \rfloor</math>, alright;<br>but for even <math>n</math>, <math>~~ m - 1 + \lceil n/2 \rceil = m ~ \mathbf{-} ~ \mathbf{1} + \lfloor n/2 \rfloor</math>.</ref>
